questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 3 weeks. Examination shows a clean-based, indurated, non-tender ulcer with a firm edge. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is present but non-tender. Darkfield microscopy is positive. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum causes primary syphilis. The classic chancre is painless, indurated with a clean base and firm rolled edges. Non-tender inguinal LAP (bubo) is characteristic. Darkfield microscopy confirms the diagnosis by visualising the spirochete.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on normal and erythematous skin. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. Indirect immunofluorescence on salt-split skin shows IgG on the epidermal (roof) side. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) shows linear IgG and C3 at BMZ on DIF. On salt-split skin, BP antibodies bind the epidermal roof (lamina lucida, against BP180/BPAG2 and BP230). EBA antibodies bind the dermal floor. Linear IgA shows linear IgA on DIF. Pemphigus shows intercellular pattern.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a verrucous plaque on the dorsum of his foot. The plaque has been slowly enlarging over 5 years. Histopathology shows Medlar bodies (sclerotic cells with thick double-walled chestnut-brown cells showing cross-wall septation). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is characterised by Medlar bodies (Copper pennies/sclerotic cells) — muriform cells that are the pathological hallmark. Caused by dematiaceous fungi (Fonsecaea, Cladophialophora, Phialophora). Mycetoma shows grains. Sporotrichosis shows asteroid bodies in tissue. Phaeohyphomycosis shows hyphae, not sclerotic cells.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on the lips and perioral region. He has had three similar episodes in the past year, each triggered by sun exposure. A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. Which of the following is the correct antiviral prophylaxis?
questions.exp: For recurrent herpes labialis, long-term prophylaxis is acyclovir 400 mg BD. Acyclovir 200 mg 5x/day is for episodic treatment of primary/recurrent disease. Valacyclovir 2 g is used for episodic treatment (single-day therapy). The Tzanck smear confirming multinucleated giant cells is consistent with HSV.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from rural India presents with hypopigmented anesthetic patches on the trunk and thickened superficial cutaneous nerves. Slit-skin smear shows AFB with a bacterial index of 3+. What is the WHO-recommended treatment regimen?
opts: Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly + Clofazimine 50 mg daily + Dapsone 100 mg daily for 12 months
Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months
Rifampicin 600 mg daily + Dapsone 100 mg daily + Clofazimine 50 mg daily for 24 months
Dapsone 100 mg daily monotherapy for 24 months
questions.exp: With BI 3+ this is multibacillary leprosy. WHO-MDT for MB leprosy: Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) + Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg daily + Clofazimine 50 mg daily for 12 months. PB leprosy uses Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging pearly nodule with telangiectasias on the nose. The lesion has a central ulcer with a rolled, pearly border. What is the most common site for this tumor and its most common histological subtype?
opts: Head and neck; nodular basal cell carcinoma
Upper limbs; superficial basal cell carcinoma
Lower limbs; infiltrative basal cell carcinoma
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is most common on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck (particularly nose). The nodular subtype is the most common histological variant, presenting as a pearly papule/nodule with telangiectasias and central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'). Superficial BCC is more common on the trunk.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with SLE presents with blistering at sun-exposed areas. DIF shows IgG, IgM, IgA, and C3 in a granular band at the DEJ — the 'full house' pattern. This finding is most characteristic of which condition?
questions.exp: The lupus band test (LBT) demonstrates granular deposits of multiple immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA) and complement at the DEJ — the 'full house' pattern. It is positive in sun-exposed skin in ~90% of SLE patients and in non-sun-exposed skin in ~60%. It is not specific to one immunoglobulin or complement alone.

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient develops a widespread erythematous maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities 2 weeks after starting amoxicillin for a throat infection. The throat swab grows Epstein-Barr virus on serology. What is this drug reaction called?
questions.exp: Aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin) cause a morbilliform rash in nearly 100% of patients with EBV infectious mononucleosis. This is not a true penicillin allergy — it is a pharmacological idiosyncrasy specific to the EBV-infected state. The mechanism involves altered immune response during EBV infection.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. Nail pitting and oil drop sign are noted. What is the pathological basis of Auspitz sign?
opts: Thinned suprapapillary epidermis with dilated dermal capillaries
questions.exp: In psoriasis, the suprapapillary epidermis is thinned (Munro's microabscess and parakeratosis above). When scales are removed, bleeding occurs from the dilated, tortuous dermal capillaries in the elongated rete ridges — this is Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding). The capillaries are fragile and superficial due to papillary elongation.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted erosions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain of the exudate shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the first-line topical treatment for limited lesions?
questions.exp: The description is of non-bullous impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus (Gram-positive cocci in clusters). Mupirocin 2% ointment is the first-line topical antibiotic for limited impetigo per most guidelines, as it covers both S. aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Fusidic acid is an alternative. Retapamulin is another option.

questions.q: A 19-year-old college student presents with a pruritic eruption in the web spaces of fingers, wrists, and genitalia. Examination reveals linear burrows and excoriations. The condition is worse at night. What is the causative organism and the treatment of choice?
opts: Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis; permethrin 5% cream
questions.exp: Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Classic features: nocturnal pruritus, linear burrows in finger web spaces/wrists/genitalia. Treatment of choice is permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down for 8-12 hours, repeated after 1 week. The whole household must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythema on the face that spares the nasolabial folds. She has photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is positive (1:320, homogeneous). Anti-dsDNA is elevated. Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the MOST SPECIFIC antibody for SLE (~99% specificity) though less sensitive (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is highly specific (~95%) but also less sensitive. Anti-dsDNA titres correlate with disease activity and lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro is more associated with Sjögren's/neonatal lupus. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presents with a rapidly spreading necrotising infection of the perineum with foul-smelling discharge, gas in the tissues on imaging, and systemic sepsis. What is this condition and what is the most critical initial management step?
opts: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; intravenous cloxacillin
Necrotising fasciitis type I; high-dose penicillin only
Gas gangrene; hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis of the perineum/genitalia with very high mortality. Risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression, alcoholism. The most critical management is immediate aggressive surgical debridement — antibiotics and supportive care alone are insufficient. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (including anaerobic coverage) are also essential.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive patient with CD4 count of 80 cells/mm³ presents with painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution over the thorax, extending to the back and chest. Two adjacent dermatomes are involved. What is the most appropriate antiviral treatment?
opts: Valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days
Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
Famciclovir 500 mg three times daily for 7 days
IV Acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7-10 days
questions.exp: In immunocompromised patients (HIV with low CD4), multidermatomal or disseminated herpes zoster carries risk of visceral/CNS dissemination. Intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) is indicated for severe/immunocompromised cases. Oral antivirals are appropriate for immunocompetent patients with localised zoster. IV route ensures adequate drug levels.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss affecting the entire scalp without scarring. She gave birth 3 months ago. Trichoscopy shows no miniaturisation. Pull test is positive with mostly telogen hairs. What is the diagnosis and expected prognosis?
opts: Telogen effluvium; self-limiting, hair regrows within 6-12 months
Anagen effluvium; hair regrows after trigger removal
questions.exp: Postpartum hair loss is classic telogen effluvium, occurring 2-4 months after delivery as hair shifts from anagen (prolonged by pregnancy oestrogens) to telogen synchronously. It is self-limiting and regrowth occurs within 6-12 months. No miniaturisation distinguishes it from AGA. Pull test shows predominantly telogen (club) hairs.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with multiple comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. He wants to start isotretinoin. Which of the following is the most important counselling point before initiating therapy?
opts: Two forms of contraception in female patients due to teratogenicity
Take the drug on an empty stomach
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic (Category X). Female patients of childbearing potential must use two forms of contraception (one primary method + one secondary method) starting 1 month before, during, and for 1 month after treatment — this is mandated by the iPLEDGE program in the US (or equivalent). Pregnancy testing is mandatory monthly. It is taken with food (fatty meal) for absorption.

questions.q: A patient presents with a hyperpigmented macule that recurs at the same site on the lip every time they take a NSAID. The macule turns dusky red during the episode and heals with residual hyperpigmentation. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) characteristically recurs at the same anatomical site with each drug exposure. It presents as a dusky red/violaceous plaque that heals with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Common sites: lips, genitalia, face. Common culprits: NSAIDs (especially nimesulide, ibuprofen), cotrimoxazole, tetracyclines, metronidazole.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with scaly plaques in the scalp with hair loss. Dermoscopy shows tubular perifollicular scales, honey-comb pattern, and red dots. Broken hairs are seen. Fluorescence under Wood's lamp shows green fluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tinea capitis (dermatophyte scalp infection) shows green fluorescence under Wood's lamp with Microsporum infections. Dermoscopy hallmarks include comma hairs, corkscrew hairs, morse-code hairs, and broken stubby hairs. In ectothrix infections (Microsporum), spores surround the hair shaft. Perifollicular scaling and cervical lymphadenopathy are characteristic.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with painful genital ulcers, bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes), and systemic fever. The ulcers are soft, purulent, and have undermined edges. Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods in a 'school of fish' pattern. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. It presents with painful, soft, purulent ulcers with undermined edges and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes that may suppurate). Gram stain shows Gram-negative coccobacilli in chains or 'school of fish' pattern. Treatment: azithromycin 1 g single dose or ceftriaxone 250 mg IM.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic tense blisters on the thighs and abdomen. Mucosal involvement is absent. ELISA shows high anti-BP180 (NC16A domain) antibodies. What is the most important prognostic marker for disease severity?
opts: Anti-BP180 antibody titres correlate with disease activity
C3 levels predict response to therapy
questions.exp: In bullous pemphigoid, anti-BP180 (anti-NC16A domain of collagen XVII) antibody titres correlate with disease extent and activity. Higher titres indicate more extensive blistering. Monitoring titres helps guide therapy. Anti-BP230 is also a target but less clinically correlative. Anti-desmoglein antibodies are for pemphigus, not BP.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with erythematous plaques in a perioral and perinasal distribution, with acneiform papules and pustules but sparing of the skin immediately adjacent to the lips (perioral pallor). He has been using a potent topical steroid on his face for 3 months. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Perioral dermatitis presents as erythematous papules and pustules around the mouth/nose/eyes with a characteristic sparing zone around the lip vermilion. Topical steroids (especially fluorinated ones) are the most common precipitant. Treatment involves stopping the steroid (rebound flare may occur), topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or oral tetracyclines.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a single well-defined hypopigmented patch on the cheek. The patch has fine scales and mild itching. Examination shows dry, scaly patches on sun-exposed areas. Wood's lamp examination shows no fluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is common in children (3-16 years), presenting as hypopigmented, poorly defined, slightly scaly patches on the face — especially cheeks. It is considered a mild eczematous condition. Wood's lamp shows no fluorescence (unlike tinea versicolor which shows yellow-orange fluorescence). It resolves spontaneously. Vitiligo shows milk-white depigmentation with accentuation under Wood's lamp.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive thickening and yellowing of all toenails with subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis. KOH preparation of subungual debris shows septate hyphae. Which organism is the most common cause of onychomycosis?
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common cause of onychomycosis (tinea unguium) worldwide, accounting for approximately 70-80% of cases. It typically causes distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO). Trichophyton mentagrophytes var. interdigitale is the second most common. Candida is more common in fingernails, especially in immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with a tender erythematous nodule on the calf with fever and raised ESR. Biopsy shows septal panniculitis with lymphocytic infiltrate but no vasculitis. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum (EN) is the most common form of panniculitis. It presents as tender erythematous nodules on the anterior shins/calves. Histology shows SEPTAL panniculitis without vasculitis — Miescher's granulomas are pathognomonic. Bilateral hilar LAP suggests sarcoidosis as the aetiology. Erythema induratum shows lobular panniculitis with vasculitis, associated with TB.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a Mohs micrographic surgery for a recurrent basal cell carcinoma on the nose. What is the key advantage of this technique over standard excision?
opts: 100% margin examination in a tissue-sparing manner
No recurrence rate with a single procedure
Shorter operating time than standard excision
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery allows complete examination of 100% of surgical margins (both peripheral and deep) in real time using horizontal frozen sections, allowing maximum tissue conservation. It is ideal for tumours on cosmetically sensitive areas (nose, eyelid, ear) and recurrent/aggressive BCCs. Standard excision examines only 1-2% of margins with vertical sections.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with episodic flushing, telangiectasias, papules, and pustules on the central face (nose, cheeks, forehead) without comedones. She reports flushing triggered by hot beverages and spicy food. What is the first-line treatment for the papulopustular component?
questions.exp: Rosacea papulopustular subtype is treated with topical metronidazole 0.75-1% (or azelaic acid 15-20%, or ivermectin 1% cream) as first-line therapy. Oral doxycycline (sub-antimicrobial dose 40 mg modified-release) is indicated for moderate-severe disease. Topical tretinoin and benzoyl peroxide can worsen rosacea by causing irritation. Comedones distinguish acne from rosacea.

questions.q: A 60-year-old presents with a rapidly growing ulcerated nodule on the pinna. Histology shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma with perineural invasion. Which of the following portends a worse prognosis?
questions.exp: High-risk features of SCC include: perineural invasion, poor differentiation, depth > 2 mm, diameter > 2 cm, location (ear, lip, non-sun-exposed), immunosuppression, and recurrence. Perineural invasion (PNI) indicates aggressive behaviour with higher rates of local recurrence, lymph node metastasis, and disease-specific mortality. Well-differentiated SCC has a better prognosis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with grouped papules and vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. He has a history of coeliac disease. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papillae tips. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is the skin manifestation of coeliac disease. DIF shows characteristic granular IgA at dermal papillae tips (pathognomonic). Treatment: dapsone provides rapid symptom relief (within 24-48 hours) and strict gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment that reduces dapsone requirement and risk of GI lymphoma.

questions.q: A newborn presents with extensive flaccid blistering over the body at birth. The blisters heal without scarring. The mother had history of pemphigus vulgaris during pregnancy with high anti-desmoglein antibody titres. What is the mechanism of neonatal pemphigus?
opts: Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG anti-desmoglein antibodies
De novo mutation in desmoglein gene
questions.exp: Neonatal pemphigus occurs when maternal IgG anti-desmoglein 1 and/or anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies cross the placenta via FcRn receptors and bind neonatal desmoglein, causing acantholysis. It is self-limiting (resolves within weeks as maternal antibodies are cleared) and requires supportive care. It correlates with maternal disease activity and antibody titres.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with well-demarcated hypopigmented macules on the chest and upper back with fine scaling. KOH mount shows short hyphae and clusters of spores (spaghetti and meatballs pattern). What is the treatment and what explains the hypopigmentation?
opts: Topical ketoconazole; azelaic acid produced by Malassezia inhibits tyrosinase
Griseofulvin; direct destruction of melanocytes by the fungus
Topical terbinafine; inflammatory damage to melanocytes
Oral fluconazole; UV-blocking by fungal scales
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor (tinea versicolor) is caused by Malassezia furfur/globosa. KOH shows the pathognomonic 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern (short hyphae + spores). Hypopigmentation results from azelaic acid produced by the fungus, which competitively inhibits tyrosinase, reducing melanin synthesis. Treatment: topical antifungals (ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione); oral fluconazole/itraconazole for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with progressive skin hardening starting from the fingers (sclerodactyly) with puffy fingers, Raynaud's phenomenon, and digital pitting scars. ANA is positive with a speckled pattern. Anti-Scl-70 is positive. Which organ complication is most life-threatening in this condition?
opts: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and interstitial lung disease
questions.exp: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc with higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis/ILD. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and ILD are the leading causes of death in SSc. Scleroderma renal crisis (SRC) can cause acute kidney injury (associated with anti-RNA polymerase III). PAH is especially associated with limited SSc (anti-centromere antibodies).
